How many pilgrims are expected in the coming months?

About 5.96 lakh pilgrims in August 2026, with the next 5 months below.

The likely range is where 90% of this model's past errors fell on ordinary months. It is not a guarantee, and it is not the range to plan a disruption against — ask about a disruption for that.

What happens to these numbers if there is a disruption?

The range widens enormously. In December 2026 a disrupted month could fall anywhere from zero to 12.01 lakh.

The ordinary range is measured on ordinary months. Months inside a declared shock window — a closure, a security shock, a landslide — behave differently, and the same model's error there is far wider. Plan a contingency against the right-hand column, not the left.

MonthOrdinary rangeIf disrupted

Every lower bound is zero. That is a measurement, not a placeholder: the record contains months when this shrine was closed and the count really was zero. The band stops at zero rather than going negative, but the floor itself is something that has happened.

These are pilgrims per month. They size what a month needs. They cannot tell you the load on any given day or hour, so they cannot identify a crush risk on a particular afternoon.

This band describes a disruption like the ones already in the record. A disruption beginning after the last observed month is in no number on this page.

Which forecasting model is best?

There isn't one. sarimax_cal is best on ordinary months and ranks 4 of 9 during disruptions; naive is best during disruptions and ranks 8 of 9 on ordinary months.

That reversal is the whole point of this project. A single leaderboard averaged over all months does not merely lose precision — it recommends the model that fails exactly when a forecast would have mattered most. Across the block-bootstrap resamples of the record, the two rankings came out inverted in 95.8% of them.

Lower is better. Rank is within its own column, and every model is scored on an identical set of forecast origins, so the two columns are directly comparable.

ModelOrdinary monthsRankDisrupted monthsRankMove

sarima1.37224.5623+1
holt_winters_add1.43135.9799+6
switching1.43545.8708+4
switching_sticky1.51655.6246+1
seasonal_naive1.52065.7247+1
theta1.96474.7605-2
naive4.15583.1331-7
drift4.19793.1472-7

The rank correlation between the two orderings is -0.383 — negative, which is what an inversion looks like. Its interval spans zero, so that single statistic on its own would not clear the conventional significance threshold: the record simply does not contain many disrupted months. The specific substitutions a planner would actually make are sharper on the same evidence, and are reported in the README.

How accurate is this, really?

On an ordinary month one step ahead, the forecast is typically within 8% of what happens. On a disrupted month it is typically out by 78%.

Half of all forecasts land inside the first figure below and half outside it, so read the last two columns too: they are the share of months that came in close.

Lead timeTypical errorWithin 10%Within 25%
1 month ahead7.8%57%92%
2 months ahead10.1%50%85%
3 months ahead10.0%50%85%
4 months ahead10.8%47%84%
5 months ahead11.3%46%81%
6 months ahead11.9%45%82%

Accuracy decays with lead time, as it should, but gently. What does not decay gently is the regime: the same model on disrupted months is out by 78% at the median, and that is the number worth carrying around. Nothing here predicts a shrine closure. What the system is worth is the range it puts around a month and its honesty about how far that range widens when things go wrong.

A note on that scale, because it is easy to misread and this page got it wrong once. The denominator is the seasonal-naive error measured inside the training window, not the error seasonal-naive posts as a forecaster. So a score above 1 does not mean the model is beaten by last-year's-same-month. Actually forecasting with last year's same month scores 1.52 on ordinary months against this model's 1.35 — the model is ahead of it, by about 11%. The number is for comparing models against each other, which is the only thing this project uses it for.

Scored on the same footing everywhere in this project: 1.35 mean MASE on ordinary months and 4.62 on disrupted ones. None of it is measured on data the model was fitted on — every figure comes from a rolling backtest of 362 separate forecast origins, each forecasting 1 to 6 months past what it was allowed to see.

Where this comes from
  • results/metrics.csv — all 2,172 scored forecasts for sarimax_cal, by regime and horizon
What counts as a disrupted month?

5 windows are declared, covering 27 months. 2 of them have been checked against their source so far.

A month is disrupted only if it falls inside one of these declared windows. Everything else is ordinary. There is no third category, and no window can be declared without a source citation — the loader refuses to start without one.

WindowWhat it wasMonthsLengthSourceChecked?
covid_closureCOVID-19 total closure and capped reopening2020-03 – 2020-108Kashmir Obserververified
covid_recovery_pre_deltaCOVID-19 recovery, first phase (pre-delta)2020-11 – 2021-035Kashmir Observernot yet audited
delta_waveCOVID-19 second (delta) wave2021-04 – 2021-063Kashmir Observernot yet audited
covid_recovery_post_deltaCOVID-19 recovery, second phase (post-delta)2021-07 – 2021-126Kashmir Observernot yet audited
floods_2025J&K security shock and monsoon landslide closure (compound)2025-05 – 2025-095Kashmir Obserververified

These labels are used only to score results. No model ever receives one. A model that could see which months were disrupted would post a spectacular result on exactly those months and mean nothing at all.

Two candidates were considered and rejected — the 2019 Article 370 period and the 2022 New Year stampede — because the monthly series shows no disruption in either. Both stay on record with the reasoning, because a window somebody examined and declined is part of the audit trail.

Is a disruption a disruption, or do different kinds behave differently?

Different kinds behave differently. 5 declared windows, 4 different winning models.

The ordinary/disrupted split is binary, and that hides the same kind of averaging this project objects to in the overall leaderboard. These windows are not variations on a theme: a cliff to zero, a slow climb, a second cliff inside that climb, and a compound security-and-landslide event.

WindowForecastsBest model hereWhere naive lands
covid_closure48naive1 of 9
covid_recovery_post_delta36drift2 of 9
covid_recovery_pre_delta30drift2 of 9
floods_202530switching7 of 9
delta_wave18seasonal_naive2 of 9

The COVID windows supply 81% of the pooled disrupted column, so the pooled answer is largely an answer about one event. On floods_2025 the winner is switching, and the pooled winner naive comes 7 of 9.

Read that comparison carefully: it rests on 1 non-COVID window. The COVID windows are one event subdivided, so every disagreement in this table involves the same 1 window again and again — it is one comparison repeated, not several independent ones. Nothing here separates different kinds of disruption need different models from floods_2025 happens to have an odd winner, and those are not the same claim. A second disruption unrelated to COVID is what would tell them apart.

This does not overturn the headline finding, it sharpens the warning. Ordinary and disrupted rankings still invert. What the table adds is narrower: the pooled disrupted leaderboard does not describe every disrupted month inside it, so "best during disruptions" is not a safe thing to read off it. Whether that is because disruptions come in kinds, or because one window in this record is unusual, is a question this site's data cannot answer.

The thinnest window carries 18 forecasts per model. No single column here is resolvable on its own, and none is offered as one. What this supports is the pattern across windows, not any cell in it.

What can this NOT tell me?

Several things, and the first matters most for crowd safety.

  • Peak-hour or peak-day load. The series is monthly throughout. Sizing a single day's barricading, queue geometry or medical cover needs daily — ideally hourly — arrival counts, and those are not in this project. A month of ordinary throughput can contain a fatal crush without the monthly total moving at all.
  • Where crowding happens. Footfall counts people entering. It is not a density anywhere on the track. Chokepoints are a site-geometry question this data cannot see.
  • Any disruption that has not started yet. The break detector reacts to a break only after it appears in observed data. A disruption beginning after the last observed month is in no number here.
  • Anything about another shrine. This is one site, and its disruptions are its own.
  • Some shock boundaries are not yet audited. 3 of the 5 declared windows (covid_recovery_pre_delta, delta_wave, covid_recovery_post_delta) carry a citation the project owner has not yet checked against its source. The regime split therefore rests in part on an unaudited boundary, and this page says so rather than waiting until it is tidy.

  • docs/operations.md — the declared limitations of the briefing
  • experiments/configs/shocks.yaml — the per-window verification flags
How many marshals, medical posts or gates do I need?

This project will not tell you, and that is deliberate.

No resourcing ratios are declared, so none are computed. Marshals per thousand pilgrims a day, medical posts, gate counts — those are site policy, set by people with operational authority and site experience. They are not model output.

A default invented here would render in the briefing table in the same typeface as one signed off by an operations lead, and no reader could tell the two apart. So the field ships empty and the briefing says so out loud.

To supply them: add them under planning.ratios in experiments/configs/operations.yaml and re-run the operations stage. The forecast volumes on this page are the input they would multiply.

Where this comes from
  • experiments/configs/operations.yaml — planning.ratios, shipped empty on purpose

487 months of published pilgrim counts, January 1986 to July 2026, with no gaps.

The counts are transcribed from the shrine board's published month-wise figures. Every row carries the source it came from, and every annual total reconciles against the sum of its own months — the pipeline refuses to run if one does not.

How are the festival dates worked out?

They are computed from an astronomical ephemeris, not looked up in a table — 966 dates across the span.

There is no hardcoded date table anywhere in this project. The positions of the sun and moon are computed, the lunar day and solar ingress are derived from them, and each festival's own civil-day rule decides which calendar date it lands on. Those rules genuinely differ — some festivals are fixed by sunrise, one by midnight, one by dusk — and which rule applies decides more dates than any disagreement between ephemerides does.

Astronomy backendskyfield
Ayanamsalahiri
Festivals tracked5
Dates resolved966

Tracked: Chaitra Navratri (day 1), Diwali (Lakshmi Puja), Maha Shivaratri, Raksha Bandhan, Sharad Navratri (day 1). These are the five that move the monthly count at this shrine, not a general almanac.

The dates are checked against published almanacs in the test suite. If they ever disagree, the fix goes to the computation, never to the test.

Does the finding survive a different boundary?

Yes. The ranking inverts under 2 of 2 different definitions of what counts as a disrupted month.

The shock windows are drawn by hand, which is the obvious place a finding like this could turn out to be an artefact. So the same forecasts are re-scored under a deliberately different set of boundaries — one window dropped for showing no signal, another trimmed, a third extended. Nothing is refitted; only the labels move, because no model ever saw a label in the first place.

Window setWindowsRank correlationStill inverts?
declared5-0.383yes
refined2-0.400yes

The correlation stays negative either way. The inversion is not an artefact of where the lines were drawn.

Did any model fail to run?

Yes — holt_winters_mul. It is reported here rather than quietly dropped from the leaderboard.

A model that cannot be fitted on part of the record is a result about the record, not a bug to hide. Dropping it from the table would be falsification, so it stays, with its reason.

ModelOrigins it could not fitFirst failure
holt_winters_mul70 of 3622020-04

The cause is the closure months. Multiplicative seasonality cannot be estimated on a series containing a zero, and this series contains several. That is a real limitation of the method on this kind of data, and it belongs in the results.

Where this comes from
  • results/applicability.csv — 1 model(s) reported unfittable
How does this whole thing work?

Forecast the past, over and over, and score what actually happened.

Every claim on this page comes out of one procedure. Pick a month in the past. Give a model only the data available up to that month. Ask it for the next six. Compare against what actually happened. Move forward one month and do it again.

Forecast origins362
Horizons per origin6
Models compared9
Forecasts scored19,548

Every model is scored on exactly the same origins against the same baseline, and the pipeline refuses to finish if any model is missing from any cell of that grid. Different origins is not a comparison.

Only then are the results split into ordinary and disrupted months and the two leaderboards compared. That split is applied afterwards, purely as a label. It never reaches a model.

Where this comes from
  • results/metrics.csv — the full origin x horizon x model grid, 19,548 rows

Neither of these is a bug, and neither has a default. Both are recorded here for the same reason they are recorded in the README: a reader should not have to find out from someone else.

  • 3 of 5 shock windows are not yet audited (covid_recovery_pre_delta, delta_wave, covid_recovery_post_delta). Their citations were drafted from public reporting and have not been checked against the sources.

Observations run January 1986 to July 2026, transcribed from the shrine board's published month-wise figures. This page is generated by make ui from results/ and is a static file: it holds no live connection to the models, and opening it runs no forecast.
